prize_parts.citation: For discoveries establishing the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and identifying its active form, enabling incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange, B006 remains the only part I would put forward, and the convergence of all six members on it is now matched by agreement on maturity: nobody has raised a doubt about the mechanism, the replication in large outcome trials, or the breadth of clinical effect. The question the chair posed is the right one, and I answer it directly. The citation should reward the discovery of GLP-1 physiology and its active form, with the therapeutic arc named as the consequence. That reading keeps the award in the Physiology or Medicine tradition of honouring a principle that opened a field, and it maps onto three separable, checkable steps: Holst on human incretin physiology, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology, receptor action and extra-pancreatic effects, and Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the insulinotropic GLP-1(7-36/37) forms. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1. What round 1 changed is how firmly I hold the third seat: I now see it as a decision the committee must make explicitly on the documentary record, not by default.
statement.case_against: The weakness is the third seat. Habener and others have a serious claim on early proglucagon and GLP-1 work and are outside the credited list, and Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is contested. I have still not checked the primary documents myself, and a prize that rests on a contested priority chain is exposed in a way that a Drucker, Holst, Knudsen citation might not be. The opposing case is also substantive: native GLP-1 has a half-life of minutes, and the medicines exist because of acylation and analogue design, so a discovery-only citation can be read as honouring the biology while leaving out the step that reached patients. I judge that this is a reason to word the citation carefully, not to change the names, but I hold that view with moderate rather than high confidence.

responses.point: The chair puts Knudsen in the trio with Drucker and Holst, arguing that a citation naming both discovery and development is more faithful to what changed medicine, and acknowledges that crediting an industry scientist departs from the usual pattern.
responses.response: I accept that your citation describes the clinical history accurately, and I agree that industry authorship is not itself a bar. My difficulty is that the development step is the engineering of a mechanism already defined by others, and putting Knudsen in the trio would displace one of the people who defined the mechanism. I think the way to honour the development arc without a third name is a citation that states that the discoveries enabled long-acting incretin therapies. To your question on priority: if the documentary record shows that Mojsov's identification of the active forms cannot be separated from or placed ahead of other groups with confidence, Knudsen becomes the right third name for me and I would vote that way. Absent that finding I stay with Mojsov.

responses.point: Sandberg says a Drucker, Holst, Mojsov trio is defensible but that Mojsov's inclusion carries more attribution risk than Knudsen's, and wants that risk examined before the final ballot.
responses.response: I agree the risk should be examined, and I would treat it as a precondition rather than a footnote. Where I differ is on the direction of the risk. A prize for a discovery that omits the person who identified and synthesised the active peptide invites a criticism of historical accuracy that is hard to answer, whereas omitting Knudsen invites a criticism of scope that a well-worded citation can partly answer. I note that you would not block my trio, and I would not block yours if the priority record turns against Mojsov. The disclosed co-authorship between us concerns single-cell work and has no bearing on this ballot.

responses.point: Perlmann keeps Mojsov and makes the same conditional: Knudsen is the natural third name only if Mojsov's priority cannot be defended. Perlmann also questions whether optogenetics is ready to rank above the unfolded protein response or CAR-T.
responses.response: We are aligned on B006 and on the condition. On optogenetics, I accept the criticism that my ranking of B002 second rested on originality and breadth more than on demonstrated medical effect, and that vision restoration is a single early example. I still keep it as an alternative because it is an invention-level advance that changed what experiments in physiology can be done. But it cannot be a lead part while the six-name credit problem is unresolved, and I would not argue for it this year. I agree with you that B016 is a clean and sound Walter and Mori award; my lower rank for it reflected the indirect disease link, not doubt about the science.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius moved B006 ahead of her opening first choice, TNF blockade (B001), and keeps it as a mature, arguably overdue achievement with a clean two-person credit.
responses.response: Your move to B006 is persuasive, and your point that a GLP-1 prize leaves TNF blockade unrewarded is fair. I still read B001 as weaker on the discovery step, because the antibody engineering and the cytokine biology sit with others outside the Feldmann and Maini credit, and I would want the committee to say what exactly the achievement is before ranking it higher. I do not see room for it as a second part within the three-person limit without cutting GLP-1 to two names, which I would not accept. As a candidate for a later year with that question answered, I take it seriously.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps Drucker, Holst and Mojsov but would accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov as the safer choice if the priority record is unclear, and wants the citation to name the therapeutic translation.
responses.response: I agree with the structure of your position, and I adopt your suggestion on the wording: the citation should name the incretin-based therapies so that Knudsen's line is recognised in the text. I would not go as far as treating Knudsen as the default whenever the record is murky, because unclear is not the same as unfavourable to Mojsov. The test I would apply is whether the record shows someone else clearly ahead of her on the active GLP-1(7-36/37) forms. If it does, I move; if it only shows parallel work, I do not.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36/37) forms against Habener and others; this is the single fact that would change my third name to Knudsen.
Whether a citation that names the therapies is enough to answer the objection that the prize omits the development step, or whether the committee would regard that as insufficient.
Whether the committee should treat the optogenetics credit problem across six names as disqualifying in any year, or only unresolved this year.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific conflict has emerged and I propose no recusal. My documented eight co-authored works with Rickard Sandberg concern single-cell work and no shortlisted candidate or credited name. My spatial-transcriptomics and single-cell background does not overlap with any credited person on B006, B019 or B002, and the first-round exchange has not changed this.
